messages.content: Argue that aesthetic value cannot be coherently reduced to purely subjective preference or individual psychological response. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) the phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience involves a claim to intersubjective validity — when we judge a work beautiful we implicitly call on others to agree, a normative dimension that a purely subjectivist framework cannot explain; (2) the practice of aesthetic criticism — with its apparatus of reasons, standards, and education — presupposes that aesthetic assessments are answerable to considerations beyond individual response, and that some responses are better-informed than others; (3) aesthetic relativism generates a regress: if every preference is equally valid, then the preference for pluralism over dogmatism is itself merely a preference, undermining the normative force of the relativist position from within. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

message.content:
Aesthetic value cannot be coherently reduced to purely subjective preference because the phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience already exceeds the structure of mere liking. When someone judges a work beautiful, moving, graceful, profound, or artistically successful, the judgment is not ordinarily experienced as a private report equivalent to “this happens to please me.” It carries an implicit appeal to others, as though the object itself merits appreciation. To call a painting beautiful is not simply to describe one’s psychological state before it; it is to present the work as worthy of admiration. The judgment therefore has a normative and intersubjective character: it asks, or at least invites, others to see what one sees. This does not mean that everyone must in fact agree, but it does mean that aesthetic judgment presents itself as more than autobiographical preference. A purely subjectivist framework can register the occurrence of pleasure, attraction, excitement, or aversion, but it cannot explain why aesthetic language so naturally takes the form of appraisal rather than confession. The difference between “I like this” and “this is beautiful” is not merely grammatical; it marks the difference between reporting an individual response and making a claim that aspires to shared recognition.

The same point is confirmed by the practice of aesthetic criticism. Criticism would be unintelligible if aesthetic assessments were nothing more than isolated psychological events. Critics do not merely announce their reactions; they give reasons, draw comparisons, invoke genre, form, proportion, originality, expressive power, historical context, technical achievement, coherence, subtlety, and depth. They attempt to show why a work succeeds or fails, and their arguments can be more or less perceptive, informed, disciplined, or shallow. The very existence of aesthetic education presupposes that taste can be cultivated and that perception can be refined. One can learn to hear structural complexity in music, to notice compositional balance in painting, to recognize dramatic economy in theater, or to appreciate allusion and rhythm in poetry. Such learning does not simply produce new private preferences; it enables better attention to features of the work. If all responses were equally authoritative merely because they occurred, there would be no meaningful distinction between a hasty reaction and a trained judgment, between inattentiveness and insight, between missing what is present in a work and responding to it with understanding. The institutions and practices of criticism therefore presuppose that aesthetic value is answerable to considerations beyond the brute fact of individual response.

Aesthetic relativism also undermines itself from within. If every aesthetic preference is equally valid simply because it is someone’s preference, then no preference can claim superiority over any other, including the preference for tolerance, pluralism, or openness. The relativist who treats all tastes as equally legitimate typically presents this stance as preferable to dogmatism, narrowness, or authoritarian judgment. But if relativism is true in the strong sense that aesthetic positions have no validity beyond the preferences of individuals or communities, then the valuation of pluralism is itself merely one preference among others. It has no greater normative standing than the dogmatism it rejects. The relativist cannot coherently say that we ought to be pluralistic, receptive, or nonjudgmental, because “ought” introduces precisely the kind of normativity that radical subjectivism dissolves. Thus the view consumes its own authority: it seeks to establish a normative conclusion while denying the grounds on which any such conclusion could be binding. Aesthetic value must therefore involve more than subjective preference, because even the attempt to deny this relies on standards of better and worse, more and less adequate, more and less defensible ways of responding.
